metadata.methods_description: EEG was acquired from 10 healthy subjects (mean age 26.8 ± 5.6 years) using 16 Ag/AgCl electrodes arranged in a 10-10 montage, referenced to linked earlobes and grounded to the right mastoid. Data were recorded with a g.USBamp amplifier at 256 Hz and processed with BCI2000 software. Visual stimuli were presented for 125 ms with 125 ms inter-stimulus intervals (250 ms stimulus onset asynchrony). Each trial consisted of 8 stimulation sequences with 16 target intensifications. Data were preprocessed with Butterworth bandpass filtering (0.1-20 Hz, order 8).

citation_details.title: Brain-Computer Interface: Current and Emerging Rehabilitation Applications
citation_details.author: Janis J. Daly, Jane E. Huggins
citation_details.venue: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
citation_details.abstract: A formal definition of brain-computer interface (BCI) is as follows: a system that acquires brain signal activity and translates it into an output that can replace, restore, enhance, supplement, or improve the existing brain signal, which can, in turn, modify or change ongoing interactions between the brain and its internal or external environment. More simply, a BCI can be defined as a system that translates "brain signals into new kinds of outputs." After brain signal acquisition, the BCI evaluates the brain signal and extracts signal features that have proven useful for task performance. There are 2 broad categories of BCIs: implantable and noninvasive, distinguished by invasively and noninvasively acquired brain signals, respectively. For this supplement, we will focus on BCIs that use noninvasively acquired brain signals.
